newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: ANALYSTS GIVE RESERVED PRAISE TO CZECH MEASURES.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS GIVE RESERVED PRAISE TO CZECH MEASURES.

text.p: Economists gave measured praise to a new austerity package unveiled by the Czech ruling coalition on Wednesday, saying it addressed the country's economic problems with needed budget cuts and wage freezes.

"On the face of it all looks like a coherent approach to minimising the trade gap, and that is the crucial priority for the government," David Lubin, emerging markets analyst at HSBC Midland, told Reuters.
"The foreign exchange crisis has been, in effect, the international financial markets' way of telling the Czech Republic 'we don't want to finance your trade deficits any more'."

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus announced a plan to freeze public sector wages, restrict public sector import demand, back the central bank's tight monetary policy, and make further budget cuts leading to a balanced budget in 1997 and a "slightly" surplus budget in 1998.

Lubin said that the steps were necessary to reduce a current account deficit -- which equals about nine percent of gross domestic product -- and take some of the pressure off the Czech crown which has fallen dramatically in recent days.
But he said there still may be volatility in trading the currency when the central bank eases its prohibitively high short-term interest rates.

The Czech crown showed little immediate reaction to the package announced late in the day, as analysts said traders was poised to pounce on the currency if the coalition would not have reached an agreement.
"These measures are all fine and dandy, but I don't think the Czech authorities have alot of credibility right now," a New York-based currency trader said.

The crown was trading on Wednesday in a tight range at about seven percent below its levels against the dollar and mark on Monday when the central bank was forced to abandon its fluctuation corridor and freely float the currency.

Klaus said that the measures, on top of an austerity package launched in April which already cut more than 20 billion crowns from the 1997 budget, would lead to an economic decline and a significant increase in unemployment.
"I think it's a good thing for the government to be up front about that," Lubin said about Klaus's gloomy forecast
"I think inevitably it's going to present political challenges just as other adjustment packages have in other emerging market countries."
